items.title: Cataract Surgery
items.shortDescription: Clearer vision begins with the right diagnosis, the right lens plan, and the right surgery for you.
longDescription: Cataract is the clouding of the natural crystalline lens, commonly associated with ageing. Surgery is the only known effective treatment for cataract removal.

At Aakash Eye Hospital, cataract surgery is focused on removing the cloudy natural lens and replacing it with an intraocular lens. Phacoemulsification with IOL implantation is the core technique used at the center.
items.imageAlt: Slit lamp examination for cataract assessment
featureBullets: Phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation
Bladeless femtosecond-assisted steps where suitable
IOL power calculation supported by advanced diagnostics
Monofocal, toric and multifocal IOLs discussed after examination

faq.question: Does cataract surgery need admission?
faq.answer: For suitable cases it is a day-care procedure: you come in, have the surgery and go home the same day. The team tells you beforehand if your case needs anything more.

faq.question: Is the surgery painful?
faq.answer: The eye is numbed before the procedure, so it is not painful. You may feel light pressure and see moving lights, and the team talks you through what is happening.

faq.question: Can both eyes be done on the same day?
faq.answer: Cataract surgery is usually planned one eye at a time. Your surgeon advises the gap before the second eye based on how the first one settles.

faq.question: Which lens will be put in my eye?
faq.answer: Monofocal, toric and multifocal intraocular lenses are all discussed with you after the examination and the lens power measurements. The right one depends on your eye and on how you use your vision.

faq.question: Will I still need glasses afterwards?
faq.answer: That depends on the lens chosen and on your eyes. Many people still use glasses for some tasks, most often for reading, and the doctor explains what to expect before you decide.

faq.question: When can I go back to normal activity?
faq.answer: Most people return to routine work quickly while continuing the prescribed drops. Your own schedule comes from the doctor at the follow-up, and it is worth planning for that visit before the day of surgery.

faq.question: What should I bring on the day?
faq.answer: Your previous case file, your current glasses, a list of the medicines you take, and someone to travel home with you.

items.title: LASIK & Refractive Surgery
items.shortDescription: Freedom from glasses begins with finding out which procedure - if any - is right for your eyes.
longDescription: LASIK is a laser procedure that can remove or reduce dependence on glasses and contact lenses for suitable patients.

Before any laser treatment the eye is mapped in detail - the shape of the cornea (topography), its thickness (pachymetry) and the eye's focusing errors (wavefront aberrometry) - to judge whether LASIK, or another option, is safe for you.
items.imageAlt: Laser surgery suite at Aakash Eye Hospital
featureBullets: Excimer laser vision correction, available since 2009
Bladeless robotic laser flap creation where suitable
Wavefront-guided diagnostic planning
ICL and refractive lens exchange discussed for higher powers

faq.question: How do I know whether LASIK will suit me?
faq.answer: Suitability is decided by tests, not by the spectacle number alone. Corneal thickness, corneal shape, the stability of your number and the general health of the eye all go into it.

faq.question: Can both eyes be treated together?
faq.answer: Both eyes are commonly treated in the same session for suitable candidates. Your surgeon confirms this after the assessment.

faq.question: Is the procedure painful?
faq.answer: Numbing drops are used, so the procedure itself is not painful. You will feel pressure for a short part of it.

faq.question: What if LASIK is not suitable for me?
faq.answer: There are other routes. ICL and refractive lens exchange are discussed where the measurements or the refractive error make laser correction unsuitable.

faq.question: When can I use screens and go back to work?
faq.answer: The doctor gives you a schedule for screens, driving and work at the follow-up, along with the drops and the protection to use in between.

faq.question: Will the number come back later?
faq.answer: Laser correction treats the number you have now. The eye still ages, so reading glasses are usually needed at some stage regardless of the surgery.

faq.question: Do I need someone to come with me?
faq.answer: Yes. Your vision will be settling afterwards, so arrange for someone to take you home.

faq.question: Why do my eyes need to be dilated?
faq.answer: Drops widen the pupil so the whole retina can be examined, not just the centre. Your vision stays blurred and light-sensitive for a few hours afterwards, so bring sunglasses and someone to travel with you.

faq.question: I have diabetes. How often should my retina be checked?
faq.answer: A retina examination is advised at least once a year, and more often if changes are already present. Your doctor sets the interval after looking at your eyes.

faq.question: What is an OCT scan?
faq.answer: A quick scan that photographs the layers of the retina. Nothing touches the eye and it takes a few minutes.

faq.question: Are the injections into the eye painful?
faq.answer: The eye is numbed first. The injection itself takes moments, and the team explains the aftercare before you leave.

faq.question: Will my vision come back after treatment?
faq.answer: That depends on the condition and on how early it is treated. Treatment often aims to protect the vision you have, and the doctor explains what is realistic for your eyes.

faq.question: Are flashes and floaters serious?
faq.answer: A few floaters are common with age. A sudden shower of new floaters, flashes of light or a shadow across your sight needs to be checked urgently.

items.title: Comprehensive Glaucoma Care
items.shortDescription: Protecting vision through early detection and long-term monitoring.
longDescription: Glaucoma is a disease where pressure inside the eye can damage the nerve fibers forming the optic nerve.

Assessment can include eye pressure measurement (applanation tonometry), visual field testing (perimetry), OCT scans of the nerve fibre layer and ganglion cells, and photographs of the optic disc and retina.
featureBullets: Pressure and optic nerve evaluation
Perimetry and OCT-supported analysis
Family history and high-risk screening guidance
Surgical care pathways when advised by the specialist

faq.question: Can glaucoma be cured?
faq.answer: Glaucoma is controlled rather than cured. Treatment aims to stop further damage to the optic nerve, which is why it continues long term.

faq.question: Does glaucoma have symptoms?
faq.answer: Usually none in the early years, which is exactly why it is found on examination rather than by how the eye feels. Some types do cause pain, redness and halos, and those need urgent care.

faq.question: Who is at higher risk?
faq.answer: A family history of glaucoma, a high spectacle number, diabetes, high blood pressure, long-term steroid use and a past eye injury all raise the risk.

faq.question: Will I lose my sight?
faq.answer: Most people who are found early and treated regularly keep useful vision for life. Missing reviews and stopping drops are what put sight at risk.

faq.question: Why do I need a field test every few months?
faq.answer: The field test is how the doctor sees whether the damage is progressing. One reading means little; the pattern over time is what guides treatment.

faq.question: Do I have to use the drops for life?
faq.answer: Usually yes, and at the same time each day. Do not stop or change them without asking the doctor, even if the eye feels completely normal.

faq.question: My parent has glaucoma. When should I be checked?
faq.answer: Earlier than someone without that history, and then at the interval the doctor advises. Mention the family history when you book.

items.title: Oculoplasty
items.shortDescription: Specialist care for eyelids, tear passages and structures around the eye.
longDescription: Oculoplasty covers the eyelids, the tear drainage passages, the orbit and the tissues surrounding the eye. Problems here can affect comfort, vision and appearance.
The team assesses the cause first and then discusses which medical or surgical options are appropriate for you.

featureBullets: Assessment of eyelid position, lumps and swellings
Watering eye and tear duct evaluation
Drooping eyelid assessment where vision is affected
Surgical options discussed after examination

faq.question: Is a watering eye always a blocked tear duct?
faq.answer: Not always. Watering has several causes, including dry eye and the position of the eyelid. The examination is what identifies the reason before any treatment is advised.

faq.question: Is this cosmetic surgery?
faq.answer: The clinic treats problems of the eyelids, the tear passages and the socket that affect how the eye works and stays protected. Where appearance is also involved, that is discussed openly with you.

faq.question: Will there be a visible scar?
faq.answer: Incisions are planned along the natural folds of the lid wherever the procedure allows. The surgeon explains what to expect for your particular case.

faq.question: Will I be asleep for the procedure?
faq.answer: Many lid and tear-duct procedures are done under local anaesthesia with you awake and comfortable. Which one suits you depends on the procedure and on your general health.

faq.question: How long does the swelling last?
faq.answer: Swelling and bruising around the lid settle gradually. The doctor gives you the expected schedule, along with when to use cold compresses and when to come back.

faq.question: Which hospital should I go to for this?
faq.answer: Availability varies between branches. Tell the appointment desk what you are noticing and the team will send you to the right one.

items.title: Pediatric Eye Care
items.shortDescription: Healthy vision plays an important role in a child's learning and development.
longDescription: Children rarely say that their vision is blurred, so many eye problems are first noticed by a parent or a teacher rather than by the child.
Examinations are adapted to a child's age and attention span, and findings are explained to the parent along with what happens next.
featureBullets: Age-appropriate vision assessment and refraction
Lazy eye (amblyopia) evaluation and follow-up
School-age eye check-ups
Referral into squint or myopia care where needed

faq.question: At what age should a child's eyes first be checked?
faq.answer: Bring a child whenever you notice something, and have the eyes checked before school even if nothing seems wrong. The doctor then sets the follow-up interval.

faq.question: My child has no complaints. Is a check-up still useful?
faq.answer: Yes. Children adapt to reduced vision without reporting it, so a routine examination often finds something the child has never mentioned.

faq.question: How do you test a child who cannot read letters?
faq.answer: There are age-appropriate tests using pictures, shapes and instruments that measure the eye directly, so a child does not need to read or even to speak.

faq.question: Do the dilating drops harm my child's eyes?
faq.answer: No. They widen the pupil so the doctor can examine and measure the eye accurately. Vision is blurred and light-sensitive for a few hours afterwards.

faq.question: Will my child need glasses for life?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Numbers change while the eye is growing, which is why the follow-up schedule matters more than any single reading.

faq.question: What is lazy eye, and can it be treated?
faq.answer: It is when one eye does not develop full vision even with glasses. It responds best to treatment when it is found early, which is the main reason for checking young children.

items.title: Myopia Clinic
items.shortDescription: Monitoring increasing spectacle numbers during childhood and adolescence.
longDescription: Short sight often begins in childhood and can change over several years. Tracking that change is what tells the team whether a plan is working.
The clinic records the measurements over time and discusses the options with the family at each review.
items.imageAlt: Trial frame refraction to measure spectacle power
featureBullets: Repeat refraction recorded over time
Review appointments scheduled by the doctor
Discussion of options with the parent at each visit
Referral into pediatric or optical services where needed

faq.question: Can the number be stopped from rising?
faq.answer: Progression can often be slowed, but an eye that has already grown does not shrink back. That is why starting early matters.

faq.question: Why does my child's number keep changing?
faq.answer: The eye is still growing. The clinic records the measurements over time so the doctor reads the pattern rather than a single visit.

faq.question: Does time outdoors really help?
faq.answer: Daylight and distance viewing are understood to help, so outdoor time and regular breaks from close work are part of what the clinic advises.

faq.question: What treatments are used besides glasses?
faq.answer: Specialised spectacle lenses, contact-lens options and prescribed eye drops are all used in myopia control. Which of them suits your child is decided after the assessment.

faq.question: How often should the eyes be rechecked?
faq.answer: At the interval the doctor sets after examination, which is usually more frequent while the number is moving quickly.

faq.question: Will my child be able to have LASIK later?
faq.answer: Laser correction is considered only once the number has been stable for a period in adulthood. Slowing the progression now keeps more options open later.

items.title: Squint Services
items.shortDescription: Assessment and treatment for eyes that are not properly aligned.
longDescription: A squint is an eye that turns inward, outward, up or down instead of aligning with the other eye. It can appear in childhood or later in life.
Assessment establishes the type and the cause, and the doctor then discusses whether glasses, exercises or surgery are appropriate.
items.imageAlt: Consulting room at Aakash Eye Hospital
featureBullets: Alignment and eye movement assessment
Refraction, because glasses correct some squints
Lazy eye assessment alongside alignment
Surgical options discussed when advised by the specialist

faq.question: Will my child grow out of a squint?
faq.answer: Some apparent squints are related to the shape of the face and some are real. An examination is what tells them apart, so it is worth checking rather than waiting.

faq.question: Is a squint only a cosmetic problem?
faq.answer: No. In children an untreated squint can hold back the vision in one eye and affect depth perception, which is why it is treated as an eye problem first.

faq.question: Can a squint be corrected with glasses alone?
faq.answer: Sometimes. Where an uncorrected number is driving the squint, glasses can do a great deal. The examination is what decides.

faq.question: Is squint treatment only for children?
faq.answer: No. Squint appears in adults too, and a new squint in an adult should be examined promptly.

faq.question: At what age is surgery done?
faq.answer: It depends on the type of squint and on the findings, not on age alone. The doctor explains the timing for your child's case.

faq.question: Does the surgery need to be repeated?
faq.answer: Sometimes more than one procedure is needed to get the alignment right. The surgeon tells you if that is likely before you decide.

faq.question: How long does a full examination take?
faq.answer: Allow longer than a quick sight test, especially if your eyes need to be dilated. The desk tells you what to plan for when you book.

faq.question: Will my eyes be dilated?
faq.answer: Often, because it is the only way to see the retina properly. Vision stays blurred and light-sensitive for a few hours, so bring sunglasses and someone to travel with you.

faq.question: How often should I have my eyes examined?
faq.answer: At least every year or two for most adults, and more often if you have diabetes, a family history of eye disease or an existing condition.

faq.question: What should I bring?
faq.answer: Your current glasses, any previous prescriptions, a list of the medicines you take and your old case file if you have one - old case files have no due date here.

faq.question: Can an eye examination pick up other health problems?
faq.answer: Sometimes. The retina is the one place where blood vessels can be seen directly, so signs of diabetes and high blood pressure can show up there.

faq.question: Do I need a referral to book?
faq.answer: No. You can book an appointment directly, and the team will guide you to the right clinic if a specialist is needed.

faq.question: Do I need an examination before new spectacles?
faq.answer: Yes. A current prescription comes from an eye examination, which also checks the health of the eye rather than only the power.

faq.question: Can I use a prescription from somewhere else?
faq.answer: Bring it with you. The optical team checks how recent it is and whether it still matches what your eyes need.

faq.question: How long will my glasses take?
faq.answer: It depends on the lens type and the frame. The optical team confirms the timing when the order is placed.

faq.question: Why do my new glasses feel strange at first?
faq.answer: A short adjustment period is normal, particularly with a changed number or a new lens type. If it does not settle in a few days, come back and have them checked.

faq.question: Do children need different frames?
faq.answer: Yes. Fit, weight and durability all matter more for a child, and a frame that slips down the nose undoes the correction.

faq.question: Is optical service available at every hospital?
faq.answer: Availability varies between branches. The appointment desk can confirm before you travel.

items.title: Emergency Eye Care
items.shortDescription: Some eye conditions require urgent evaluation.
longDescription: Sudden loss of vision, injury, chemical exposure and severe pain are reasons to seek care immediately rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

Guidance by phone before you travel
Chemical exposure: begin irrigation immediately, then call

faq.question: What should I do if a chemical enters the eye?
faq.answer: Begin flushing the eye immediately with plenty of clean water and keep going. Do not wait to call first - start the irrigation, then arrange to get here.

faq.question: Should I wait for the OPD if my vision drops suddenly?
faq.answer: No. A sudden loss or reduction of vision needs to be assessed urgently. Call the helpline straight away.

faq.question: Something hit my eye. What should I not do?
faq.answer: Do not rub the eye, do not press on it and do not try to remove anything that is stuck in it. Shield the eye if you can and come in.

faq.question: Is a red eye always an emergency?
faq.answer: No. Redness with severe pain, reduced vision or after an injury is urgent. Redness on its own can usually wait for a routine appointment.

faq.question: I had surgery recently and the eye is painful. What now?
faq.answer: Contact the hospital straight away. New pain or a drop in vision after eye surgery is always assessed urgently.

faq.question: What should I bring in an emergency?
faq.answer: Whatever is to hand: your previous records, the drops or medicines you are using, and your spectacles. Do not delay coming in to look for them.
